decks.title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes — Part 1: Structure, naming, preparation and physical properties
goals: Classify halogen compounds and name them by IUPAC rules
Describe the polarity, length and strength of the C–X bond
Write methods of preparing haloalkanes and haloarenes from alcohols, hydrocarbons and by halogen exchange
Explain trends in boiling point, density and solubility

slides.heading: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — organic compounds in which a halogen atom replaces hydrogen: how they are named, made and how they behave physically.

rows: Old refrigerants; damage the ozone layer

visual.alt: Table of familiar halogen compounds and their uses

slides.narration: Namaste! Pipes made of PVC, anaesthetics used in surgery, some antibiotics and the old refrigerants that damaged the ozone layer all contain carbon bonded to a halogen. When a halogen replaces a hydrogen atom of an alkane we get a haloalkane; when it replaces a hydrogen of an aromatic ring, a haloarene. In this part we classify and name them, see how to make them, and explain their physical properties.

slides.heading: Classifying halogen compounds
slides.body_md: By the **number of halogen atoms** (mono-, di-, poly-) and by the **type of carbon** bearing the halogen.

rows: sp³ C joined to one other C
sp³ C joined to two C
sp³ C joined to three C
sp³ C next to a C=C
sp³ C next to a benzene ring
sp² C of a benzene ring

visual.alt: Table classifying halogen compounds as primary, secondary, tertiary, allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides with examples

slides.narration: We sort halogen compounds by the carbon atom that carries the halogen. If it is an sp three carbon, we have alkyl halides, which are primary, secondary or tertiary depending on how many other carbons are attached, as well as allylic and benzylic halides next to a double bond or a ring. If the halogen sits on an sp two carbon of a double bond or a benzene ring, we have vinylic or aryl halides, which behave very differently.

slides.heading: Naming halogen compounds
slides.body_md: In IUPAC names the halogen is a **prefix** (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo) with a locant on the longest chain. Common names use the alkyl group + halide.

visual.alt: Table of common and IUPAC names of seven halogen compounds

slides.narration: In IUPAC names, the halogen is written as a prefix, such as chloro or bromo, with a number showing its position on the longest chain. So isopropyl chloride is two-chloropropane, and tert-butyl bromide is two-bromo-two-methylpropane. When two halogens are on neighbouring carbons they are called vicinal; when both are on the same carbon, geminal. Benzyl chloride is named as chloromethyl benzene.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming and classifying
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name and classify (a) $\ce{CH3CH2CH(Cl)CH3}$, (b) $\ce{(CH3)2C(Br)CH2CH3}$, (c) $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH2Br}$, (d) 1,4-dichlorobenzene.

**(a)** 2-Chlorobutane — secondary alkyl halide.

**(b)** 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane — tertiary alkyl halide.

**(c)** 1-Bromobut-2-ene — allylic halide (C–Br carbon next to C=C).

**(d)** 1,4-Dichlorobenzene (p-dichlorobenzene) — aryl dihalide.

Classify by the carbon bearing X

visual.alt: Flow for naming and classifying a halogen compound: longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical prefixes, then classify the carbon bearing the halogen

slides.narration: Work step by step. Find the longest carbon chain, number it so the substituents get the lowest numbers, and list prefixes alphabetically. Then look at the carbon carrying the halogen. In the first example, it has two carbon neighbours, so it is secondary. In the second, three, so it is tertiary. In the third, it is next to a double bond, so it is allylic.

slides.heading: The carbon–halogen bond
slides.body_md: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is **polar**: carbon is δ+ and is attacked by **nucleophiles**.

slides.narration: Every chemical property of haloalkanes comes from this bond. The halogen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, so the carbon carries a small positive charge and the halogen a small negative charge. Electron-rich species called nucleophiles are attracted to that positive carbon. That is why the typical reaction of haloalkanes is nucleophilic substitution, which we study in Part 2.

slides.heading: Bond length and bond strength
slides.body_md: Down the group the halogen atom gets larger, so the C–X bond becomes **longer and weaker**; C–I bonds break most easily.

visual.alt: Table of carbon–halogen bond lengths, bond enthalpies and dipole moments of the halomethanes

slides.narration: Look at the trend. From fluorine to iodine, the bond gets longer and much weaker, from about four hundred and fifty to about two hundred and thirty kilojoules per mole. So iodoalkanes react fastest, because their carbon–iodine bond breaks most easily. Dipole moments do not follow electronegativity simply, because longer bonds partly compensate for smaller charges.

slides.heading: Preparation from alcohols
slides.body_md: The –OH group of an alcohol is replaced by a halogen using HX, phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride. **Thionyl chloride** is preferred: its by-products are gases, leaving pure haloalkane.

rows: 1° and 2° alcohols; 3° react with conc. HCl at room temperature
Best: SO₂ and HCl escape as gases

visual.alt: Table of reagents for converting alcohols into haloalkanes with notes on each

slides.narration: Alcohols are the commonest starting point. Hydrogen chloride needs anhydrous zinc chloride as a catalyst for primary and secondary alcohols, while tertiary alcohols react readily even without it. Phosphorus trichloride and pentachloride also work well. Best of all is thionyl chloride, because its by-products, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride, are gases that simply escape, leaving the chloroalkane almost pure.

slides.heading: Preparation from hydrocarbons and diazonium salts
slides.body_md: **Alkanes:** free-radical halogenation gives mixtures. **Alkenes:** add HX (Markovnikov’s rule; with HBr and peroxide, anti-Markovnikov) or X₂. **Arenes:** electrophilic substitution with a Lewis acid gives o- and p-isomers. **Diazonium salts:** Sandmeyer reaction.

visual.alt: Table of preparations of halogen compounds from alkenes, arenes and diazonium salts

slides.narration: Hydrocarbons are another source. Halogenating alkanes in light gives messy mixtures, so it is rarely useful. Hydrogen bromide adds to propene to give two-bromopropane, following Markovnikov’s rule, but with peroxide present it gives one-bromopropane instead. Benzene reacts with chlorine only with a Lewis acid catalyst. And aryl halides are neatly made from diazonium salts by the Sandmeyer reaction.

slides.heading: Halogen exchange
slides.body_md: **Finkelstein reaction:** chloro- or bromoalkanes react with NaI in dry acetone to give iodoalkanes; NaCl and NaBr are insoluble in acetone and precipitate, driving the reaction forward. **Swarts reaction:** heating with AgF, Hg₂F₂ or SbF₃ gives fluoroalkanes.

visual.alt: Table of the Finkelstein and Swarts halogen exchange reactions

slides.narration: Iodo and fluoro compounds are made by swapping halogens. In the Finkelstein reaction, a chloroalkane is stirred with sodium iodide in dry acetone. Sodium chloride does not dissolve in acetone, so it precipitates and pulls the reaction forward. In the Swarts reaction, metal fluorides such as silver fluoride replace chlorine or bromine by fluorine.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing a preparation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Suggest a method for each conversion: (a) propan-2-ol → 2-chloropropane with a pure product; (b) propene → 1-bromopropane; (c) bromoethane → iodoethane; (d) aniline → chlorobenzene.

**(a)** $\ce{SOCl2}$ (by-products are gases).

**(b)** HBr in the presence of a peroxide (anti-Markovnikov).

**(c)** NaI in dry acetone (Finkelstein).

**(d)** $\ce{NaNO2 + HCl}$ at 273–278 K to make the diazonium salt, then CuCl/HCl (Sandmeyer).

visual.alt: Table of four conversions and the method chosen for each

slides.narration: Match the method to the task. For a pure chloroalkane from an alcohol, thionyl chloride is the clean choice. To put bromine on the end carbon of propene, add hydrogen bromide with a peroxide. To make an iodoalkane, use the Finkelstein reaction. And to turn aniline into chlorobenzene, first make the diazonium salt in the cold, then treat it with copper one chloride.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Haloalkanes are polar, so they have **higher boiling points** than alkanes of similar mass. Boiling point rises with the size of the halogen and the chain length, and falls with **branching** (smaller surface area). Bromo- and iodo-compounds are **denser than water**. They are only slightly soluble in water but dissolve well in organic solvents.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of the halomethanes rising from fluoromethane to iodomethane

slides.narration: Haloalkanes boil higher than alkanes of similar size, because their molecules are polar and larger. Among halomethanes, boiling point rises from fluoro to iodo as the molecules get heavier and more polarisable. Bromo and iodo compounds sink in water. They dissolve only slightly in water: breaking water’s hydrogen bonds costs more energy than is returned by the weaker attractions to the haloalkane.

slides.heading: Worked example: boiling points of isomers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in order of increasing boiling point: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

**Step 1.** All have the formula $\ce{C4H9Br}$, so molar mass is equal.

**Step 2.** More branching → more compact, spherical molecules → smaller contact area → weaker van der Waals forces.

**Step 3.** Order: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (346 K) < 2-bromobutane (364 K) < 1-bromobutane (375 K).

visual.alt: Table of three bromobutane isomers with their degree of branching and boiling points

slides.narration: All three isomers have the same formula and mass, so the difference must come from shape. The straight-chain one-bromobutane has the largest surface for molecules to touch, so the attractions are strongest and it boils highest. The highly branched two-bromo-two-methylpropane is almost spherical, touches its neighbours least, and boils lowest.

slides.heading: Melting points of dichlorobenzenes
slides.body_md: The three dichlorobenzenes boil at similar temperatures, but the **para** isomer melts much higher: its symmetrical molecules **pack better** in the crystal.

rows: Symmetrical, packs closely in the solid

visual.alt: Table of melting points of ortho, meta and para dichlorobenzene showing the much higher melting point of the para isomer

slides.narration: Melting depends on how well molecules fit together in a crystal. Para-dichlorobenzene is symmetrical, so its molecules stack neatly like bricks, and more energy is needed to break the lattice. It is a solid at room temperature, used in moth balls, while the ortho and meta isomers are liquids.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Classify by the carbon bearing X: 1°, 2°, 3°, allylic, benzylic (sp³); vinylic, aryl (sp²).
IUPAC: halogen as prefix with locant; vic and gem dihalides.
C–X is polar (C δ+); bond length increases and strength decreases from F to I.
From alcohols: HX/ZnCl₂, PCl₃, PCl₅, SOCl₂ (best); from alkenes: HX (Markovnikov, peroxide effect); arenes: X₂/FeX₃; Sandmeyer; Finkelstein and Swarts exchange.
Boiling point rises with mass and falls with branching; RBr and RI are denser than water; slightly soluble in water.

visual.alt: Summary table of preparations and key reagents

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. We classify halogen compounds by the carbon that carries the halogen, and name them with halogen prefixes. The carbon–halogen bond is polar and gets longer and weaker down the group. We can make these compounds from alcohols, alkenes, arenes and diazonium salts, or by halogen exchange. Their boiling points depend on size and branching, and the heavier ones sink in water.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write full balanced equations with conditions (ZnCl₂, FeCl₃, dry acetone, peroxide).
Explain why SOCl₂ is preferred: gaseous by-products.
For Finkelstein, mention that NaCl/NaBr precipitate in acetone.
For boiling points of isomers, mention surface area and van der Waals forces.
Do not confuse allylic (next to C=C) with vinylic (on C=C).

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Always write the conditions with your equations. Give the reason why thionyl chloride is the best reagent. For the Finkelstein reaction, say why it goes to completion. Remember that the peroxide effect works only with hydrogen bromide. And keep allylic and vinylic halides apart: one is next to the double bond, the other is on it.

slides.heading: Reactions of halogen compounds
slides.body_md: Part 2 — substitution, elimination and reactions with metals, and why aryl halides are so unreactive.

visual.alt: Flow: a haloalkane can undergo nucleophilic substitution, elimination to an alkene or reaction with metals

slides.narration: Haloalkanes are the workhorses of organic synthesis. Their polar carbon–halogen bond lets us swap the halogen for almost any group, remove it with a hydrogen to make an alkene, or join carbon chains using metals. In this part we study how these reactions happen, step by step, and why the same halogen on a benzene ring is so much harder to replace.

slides.heading: Nucleophilic substitution
slides.body_md: A nucleophile replaces the halogen: $\ce{Nu- + R-X -> R-Nu + X-}$. **Ambident** nucleophiles such as $\ce{CN-}$ and $\ce{NO2-}$ can attack through either of two atoms.

visual.alt: Table of nucleophilic substitution reagents, the attacking nucleophile and the product formed

slides.narration: In nucleophilic substitution, an electron-rich species pushes out the halide ion and takes its place. Hydroxide gives an alcohol, alkoxide an ether, ammonia an amine. Cyanide is interesting: with ionic potassium cyanide, the carbon end attacks and a nitrile forms; with covalent silver cyanide, the nitrogen end attacks and an isocyanide forms. Nitrite behaves similarly, giving nitrites or nitroalkanes.

slides.heading: The SN2 mechanism
slides.body_md: **S**ubstitution, **N**ucleophilic, **bi**molecular: one step. The nucleophile attacks from the side **opposite** the halogen while the C–X bond breaks. Rate $= k[\ce{RX}][\ce{Nu-}]$ (second order). The configuration is **inverted**. Reactivity: $\ce{CH3X}$ > 1° > 2° > 3° (bulky groups block the backside).

visual.alt: Table of relative SN2 rates for methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary halides with the steric reason

slides.narration: In the S N two mechanism, everything happens in a single step. The nucleophile must reach the carbon from the back, directly opposite the leaving halogen. Both species are involved in this step, so the rate depends on both concentrations. Bulky groups around the carbon get in the way, so methyl and primary halides react fastest and tertiary halides hardly at all by this route.

slides.heading: SN2: backside attack and inversion
slides.body_md: In the transition state the carbon is partly bonded to both the nucleophile and the leaving group, with the other three groups in a plane. As the halide leaves, the three groups flip over: **Walden inversion**.

visual.alt: SN2 reaction of hydroxide with bromomethane: backside attack, a transition state with the three hydrogens in one plane, and an inverted product with bromide leaving
visual.caption: Schematic; the inversion is like an umbrella turning inside out in the wind.

slides.narration: Follow the picture from left to right. Hydroxide approaches the carbon from the side away from bromine. In the middle, the transition state, the oxygen–carbon bond is half formed and the carbon–bromine bond half broken, and the three hydrogens lie flat. Then bromide leaves, and the hydrogens flip to the other side, like an umbrella turned inside out by the wind. If the carbon were chiral, its configuration would be inverted.

slides.heading: The SN1 mechanism
slides.body_md: **Uni**molecular, two steps: (1) slow ionisation to a **carbocation**; (2) fast attack by the nucleophile. Rate $= k[\ce{RX}]$ (first order). Favoured for **3°** halides (stable carbocations) and in **polar protic** solvents (water, alcohols). Allylic and benzylic halides also react fast (resonance-stabilised carbocations).

visual.alt: Flow of the SN1 mechanism: slow ionisation to a carbocation, then fast attack by the nucleophile

slides.narration: The S N one mechanism is a two-step process. First, the carbon–halogen bond breaks on its own to give a carbocation; this slow step sets the rate, which depends only on the haloalkane. Then the nucleophile quickly joins the carbocation. Tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so tertiary halides react fastest this way, especially in polar solvents like water that help the ions separate.

slides.heading: SN1 versus SN2
slides.body_md: The two mechanisms differ in every respect.
columns:
**SN2**

- One step, no intermediate
- Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]
- Order of reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°
- Inversion of configuration
- Favoured by strong nucleophiles, polar aprotic solvents

**SN1**

- Two steps via a carbocation
- Rate = k[RX]
- Order of reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X
- Racemisation (mostly) at a chiral centre
- Favoured by polar protic solvents, stable carbocations

visual.alt: Table comparing SN1 and SN2 mechanisms by steps, kinetics, best substrate and stereochemistry

slides.narration: Put the two mechanisms side by side. S N two is one step, second order, fastest for methyl and primary halides, and inverts the configuration. S N one goes through a carbocation, is first order, fastest for tertiary halides, and because the flat carbocation can be attacked from either face, a chiral starting material gives a nearly racemic product.

slides.heading: Stereochemistry: chirality and optical activity
slides.body_md: A carbon with four different groups is **chiral**; such a molecule and its mirror image (**enantiomers**) are non-superimposable and rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions (**dextro** +, **laevo** −). A 1 : 1 mixture (**racemic mixture**) is optically inactive.

rows: Equal amounts of both enantiomers; no net rotation
Product has the same configuration as the reactant

visual.alt: Table of stereochemical terms: chiral centre, enantiomers, racemic mixture, retention and inversion

slides.narration: Your hands are mirror images that do not fit on top of each other: they are chiral. A carbon atom with four different groups makes a molecule chiral too. The two mirror-image forms, called enantiomers, rotate polarised light in opposite directions. An equal mixture of both, a racemic mixture, shows no rotation. S N two gives inversion; S N one gives mostly racemisation.

slides.heading: Worked example: which reacts faster?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In each pair, which reacts faster in the stated mechanism? (a) SN2: 1-bromobutane or 2-bromobutane; (b) SN1: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane or 2-bromobutane; (c) SN1: $\ce{C6H5CH2Cl}$ or $\ce{C6H5CH(CH3)Cl}$.

**(a)** 1-Bromobutane: primary, less crowded.

**(b)** 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane: tertiary carbocation is more stable.

**(c)** $\ce{C6H5CH(CH3)Cl}$: secondary benzylic carbocation, stabilised by both the ring and the methyl group.

visual.alt: Table of the three pairs, the faster compound and the reason

slides.narration: Decide first which mechanism is asked. For S N two, ask how crowded the carbon is: the primary bromide wins. For S N one, ask how stable the carbocation is: the tertiary bromide wins. In the last pair, both give benzylic carbocations stabilised by the ring, but the one with an extra methyl group is more stable still, so it reacts faster.

slides.heading: Quick check: mechanism
slides.body_md: Identify the mechanism from rate data and stereochemistry.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use two clues: does the rate depend on the nucleophile, and is the configuration inverted or scrambled?

slides.heading: Elimination and Saytzeff’s rule
slides.body_md: With **alcoholic KOH**, a hydrogen from the β-carbon and the halogen are removed to form an alkene (**β-elimination**). **Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule:** the **more substituted alkene** (fewer H on the double-bond carbons) is the major product.

visual.alt: Table of two elimination reactions with the major and minor alkene products by Saytzeff’s rule

slides.narration: When a haloalkane is heated with potassium hydroxide in alcohol instead of water, the hydroxide acts as a base. It pulls off a hydrogen from the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen, and the halide leaves, forming a double bond. If there is a choice, the more substituted alkene, with more alkyl groups on the double bond, forms in larger amount. This is Saytzeff’s rule.

slides.heading: Substitution or elimination?
slides.body_md: Nucleophiles are also bases, so substitution and elimination compete.

rows: Good nucleophile, weak base (e.g. I⁻, CN⁻)

visual.alt: Table of conditions favouring substitution or elimination

slides.narration: Because a nucleophile is also a base, substitution and elimination are always in competition. Primary halides with aqueous hydroxide mostly give substitution. Tertiary halides with alcoholic hydroxide and heat mostly give elimination, because the crowded carbon is hard to attack but its hydrogens are easy to remove. Bulky strong bases favour elimination.

slides.heading: Reactions with metals
slides.body_md: **Grignard reagents** form with Mg in dry ether and are destroyed by water. **Wurtz reaction:** two alkyl halides join with Na in dry ether. **Wurtz–Fittig** joins an aryl and an alkyl halide; **Fittig** joins two aryl halides.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of halogen compounds with metals: Grignard, Wurtz, Wurtz–Fittig and Fittig

slides.narration: Haloalkanes react with metals in dry ether. Magnesium gives Grignard reagents, very useful for making new carbon–carbon bonds, but so reactive that even a trace of water destroys them, giving an alkane. Sodium joins two alkyl groups in the Wurtz reaction, an aryl and an alkyl group in the Wurtz–Fittig reaction, or two aryl groups in the Fittig reaction.

slides.heading: Why haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution
slides.body_md: In chlorobenzene a lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the ring, so the C–Cl bond has **partial double-bond character** and is shorter and stronger. The carbon is **sp²** (more electronegative), the phenyl cation is **unstable**, and the electron-rich ring **repels** nucleophiles.

slides.narration: Try to replace the chlorine of chlorobenzene with hydroxide in the way that works for chloroethane, and almost nothing happens. One lone pair of chlorine spreads into the ring, as these resonance structures show, so the carbon–chlorine bond is partly double, shorter and harder to break. The phenyl cation would be very unstable, ruling out S N one, and the cloud of ring electrons keeps nucleophiles away, ruling out S N two.

slides.heading: Reactions of haloarenes
slides.body_md: Replacement of Cl needs severe conditions, unless **electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂) at ortho/para** positions help. In **electrophilic substitution**, the halogen is **deactivating** (–I effect) but **ortho/para directing** (+R effect); the para product usually predominates.

visual.alt: Table of electrophilic substitution reactions of chlorobenzene and their ortho and para products

slides.narration: Haloarenes do give substitution of the halogen, but only at about six hundred and twenty three kelvin and three hundred atmospheres, as in the old industrial route to phenol. Nitro groups at ortho or para positions make it much easier by pulling electron density away. In electrophilic substitution, chlorine slows the ring down overall but directs the new group to ortho and para positions, with para usually the major product.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting products
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the main organic product: (a) 1-bromopropane + aqueous KOH; (b) 2-bromopropane + alcoholic KOH, heat; (c) bromobenzene + bromomethane + Na in dry ether; (d) chlorobenzene + Cl₂ with anhydrous FeCl₃; (e) iodomethane + AgNO₂.

**(a)** Propan-1-ol. **(b)** Propene. **(c)** Toluene (methylbenzene). **(d)** 1,4-Dichlorobenzene (major) and 1,2-dichlorobenzene. **(e)** Nitromethane.

visual.alt: Table of five reactions, their type and product

slides.narration: First identify the reaction type from the conditions. Aqueous hydroxide on a primary halide gives substitution, so an alcohol. Alcoholic hydroxide with heat gives elimination, so an alkene. Sodium with an aryl and an alkyl halide is the Wurtz–Fittig reaction, giving toluene. Chlorine with a Lewis acid substitutes the ring at ortho and para positions. Silver nitrite attacks through nitrogen, giving a nitroalkane.

slides.heading: Quick check: haloarene reactivity
slides.body_md: Explain why chlorobenzene is less reactive than chloroethane towards nucleophiles.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what resonance does to the carbon–chlorine bond in chlorobenzene.

slides.heading: Polyhalogen compounds
slides.body_md: Compounds with several halogen atoms have important uses, but many are harmful to health or the environment.

rows: Harms the nervous system; skin and eye irritant
Air oxidises it to poisonous phosgene; kept in dark, full bottles
Persistent; builds up in food chains

visual.alt: Table of six polyhalogen compounds with their uses and hazards

slides.narration: Several polyhalogen compounds deserve special mention. Chloroform slowly reacts with air in light to form phosgene, a deadly gas, so it is stored in dark bottles filled to the top. Iodoform is an antiseptic because it releases iodine. Freons are unreactive and non-toxic, which made them popular refrigerants, but in the upper atmosphere they release chlorine atoms that destroy ozone. DDT controls malaria mosquitoes but persists and builds up in food chains.

slides.heading: Quick check: polyhalogen compounds
slides.body_md: Explain why compounds that are safe to use at ground level can still harm the ozone layer.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what happens to a very stable compound that does not break down in the lower atmosphere.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Nucleophilic substitution: OH⁻ → alcohol, RO⁻ → ether, KCN → nitrile, AgCN → isocyanide, KNO₂ → nitrite, AgNO₂ → nitroalkane.
SN2: one step, second order, inversion, CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°. SN1: carbocation, first order, racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°.
Elimination with alc. KOH; Saytzeff: more substituted alkene is major.
Grignard (Mg, dry ether), Wurtz, Wurtz–Fittig, Fittig.
Haloarenes: C–Cl partial double bond; o/p-directing but deactivating in electrophilic substitution.
Polyhalogen compounds: CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ (phosgene), CHI₃, CCl₄, freons (ozone), DDT (persistence).

visual.alt: Summary table of the SN1 and SN2 rate laws and stereochemistry

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution by two mechanisms: S N two in one step with inversion, favoured for primary halides, and S N one through a carbocation, favoured for tertiary halides. With alcoholic hydroxide they eliminate to alkenes following Saytzeff’s rule. With metals they form Grignard reagents or join up. Haloarenes resist substitution but undergo ortho and para electrophilic substitution, and several polyhalogen compounds are useful but hazardous.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Say "aqueous KOH" for substitution and "alcoholic KOH" for elimination.
For SN1/SN2 questions, give both the rate law and the stereochemical outcome.
Ambident nucleophiles: K⁺ salts attack through C or O; Ag salts through N.
Explain haloarene inertness with resonance, sp² carbon and phenyl cation instability.
For chloroform storage, mention phosgene and dark, completely filled bottles.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some final tips. Always specify aqueous or alcoholic potassium hydroxide, because they give different reactions. In mechanism answers, give both the rate law and the stereochemistry. Learn which salts of cyanide and nitrite attack through which atom. When asked why haloarenes are unreactive, give the resonance argument first. And for chloroform, mention phosgene and how the bottles are stored.

sections.heading: 1. Classification, nomenclature and the C–X bond
sections.body_md:
**Classification:** by the number of halogens (mono-, di-, poly-) and by the carbon bearing X — sp³: primary, secondary, tertiary alkyl, allylic, benzylic; sp²: vinylic, aryl. Dihalides: **geminal** (same C, e.g. 1,1-dichloroethane) and **vicinal** (adjacent C, e.g. 1,2-dibromoethane).

**Naming:** halogen as a prefix with a locant — bromoethane, 2-chloropropane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, 3-chloroprop-1-ene (allyl chloride), (chloromethyl)benzene (benzyl chloride), 1,4-dichlorobenzene.

**C–X bond:** polar (C δ+, X δ−); bond length C–F 139 < C–Cl 178 < C–Br 193 < C–I 214 pm; bond enthalpy decreases F (452) > Cl (351) > Br (293) > I (234 kJ mol⁻¹), so reactivity is R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.

sections.heading: 2. Preparation
sections.body_md:
**From alcohols:** $\ce{ROH + HCl ->[ZnCl2] RCl + H2O}$ (3° alcohols react with conc. HCl alone); $\ce{3ROH + PCl3 -> 3RCl + H3PO3}$; $\ce{ROH + PCl5 -> RCl + POCl3 + HCl}$; $\ce{ROH + SOCl2 -> RCl + SO2 + HCl}$ (best, gaseous by-products). PBr₃ and PI₃ are made in situ from red P and Br₂ or I₂.

**From hydrocarbons:** free-radical halogenation of alkanes (mixtures); HX addition to alkenes (Markovnikov; HBr with peroxide gives anti-Markovnikov); X₂ addition gives vic-dihalides; arenes + X₂ with FeX₃ (dark) give o- and p-haloarenes.

**Sandmeyer reaction:** $\ce{C6H5N2Cl ->[CuCl/HCl] C6H5Cl + N2}$ (also CuBr/HBr).

**Halogen exchange:** Finkelstein $\ce{RCl + NaI ->[acetone] RI + NaCl}$ (NaCl precipitates); Swarts $\ce{CH3Br + AgF -> CH3F + AgBr}$ (also Hg₂F₂, CoF₂, SbF₃).

sections.heading: 3. Physical properties
sections.body_md:
- Higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass (polarity, larger size). For the same alkyl group: RF < RCl < RBr < RI. For isomers, branching lowers bp: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (346 K) < 2-bromobutane (364 K) < 1-bromobutane (375 K).
- Density increases with the number and mass of halogen atoms; bromo- and iodo-compounds are denser than water.
- Only slightly soluble in water (energy to break H-bonds in water is not compensated); soluble in organic solvents.
- p-Dichlorobenzene (mp 323 K) melts higher than o- (256 K) and m- (249 K) isomers because its symmetrical molecules pack better.

key_terms.definition_md: Weak attractions between molecules that increase with molecular size and surface area.

sections.heading: 4. Nucleophilic substitution: SN1 and SN2
sections.body_md:
**Products:** aq. KOH → alcohol; NaOR → ether; KCN → nitrile (via C); AgCN → isocyanide (via N); KNO₂ → alkyl nitrite (via O); AgNO₂ → nitroalkane (via N); NH₃ → amine; LiAlH₄ → alkane; R′COOAg → ester.

**SN2:** one step; backside attack; rate $= k[\ce{RX}][\ce{Nu-}]$; **inversion** (Walden inversion); reactivity CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance).

**SN1:** two steps via a **carbocation**; rate $= k[\ce{RX}]$; mostly **racemisation**; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X; favoured by polar protic solvents; allylic and benzylic halides react fast (resonance-stabilised carbocations).

**Stereochemistry:** a carbon with four different groups is chiral; enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally and oppositely (d/+, l/−); a racemic mixture is optically inactive. Retention: same configuration; inversion: opposite configuration.

sections.heading: 5. Elimination, reactions with metals and reactions of haloarenes
sections.body_md:
**Elimination:** alcoholic KOH removes HX (β-elimination); **Saytzeff rule** — the more substituted alkene is the major product (2-bromobutane → but-2-ene major). Strong bulky bases and 3° halides favour elimination.

**Metals:** $\ce{RX + Mg ->[dry ether] RMgX}$ (Grignard; water gives RH); **Wurtz** $\ce{2RX + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX}$; **Wurtz–Fittig** ArX + RX + 2Na → Ar–R; **Fittig** 2ArX + 2Na → Ar–Ar.

**Haloarenes** are much less reactive to nucleophilic substitution: resonance gives C–X partial double-bond character; sp² carbon; unstable phenyl cation; repulsion by the π cloud. Severe conditions are needed ($\ce{C6H5Cl + 2NaOH ->[623 K, 300 atm] C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O}$) unless –NO₂ groups occupy o/p positions. In **electrophilic substitution** the halogen is deactivating (–I) but **o/p-directing** (+R): nitration, halogenation, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts reactions give o- and p- products (p major).

key_terms.definition_md: In dehydrohalogenation, the alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons is the major product.

sections.heading: 6. Polyhalogen compounds
sections.body_md:
- **Dichloromethane:** solvent, paint remover, propellant; affects the central nervous system.
- **Trichloromethane (chloroform):** solvent; once an anaesthetic. Oxidised by air in light to poisonous **phosgene**, $\ce{2CHCl3 + O2 -> 2COCl2 + 2HCl}$, so stored in dark, completely filled bottles.
- **Triiodomethane (iodoform):** yellow solid, antiseptic due to liberated iodine; objectionable smell.
- **Tetrachloromethane:** formerly a solvent and in refrigerant manufacture; causes liver damage; ozone depleting.
- **Freons (CFCs):** refrigerants and propellants; stable, but in the stratosphere release Cl atoms that destroy ozone.
- **DDT:** insecticide used against malaria-carrying mosquitoes; not biodegradable, accumulates in fatty tissue and food chains; banned or restricted in many countries.

key_terms.definition_md: Carbonyl chloride, COCl₂, a very poisonous gas formed when chloroform is oxidised by air.
Chlorofluorocarbons used as refrigerants and propellants; they deplete stratospheric ozone.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using aqueous KOH when elimination is asked (use alcoholic KOH) or vice versa.
- Writing isocyanide for KCN (it gives a nitrile; AgCN gives an isocyanide).
- Giving the SN1 order of reactivity for an SN2 question.
- Saying SN1 gives inversion (it gives mostly racemisation).
- Calling a halogen on benzene meta-directing (it is ortho/para-directing though deactivating).
- Forgetting "dry ether" for Grignard and Wurtz reactions.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: product, reagent, name or order.
- Conversions (2–3 marks): reagent and condition for each step (½–1 each) + correct intermediate.
- Mechanism answers: rate law (½), steps or transition state (1), stereochemistry (½–1).
- Reasoning (2 marks): fact + reason (resonance, steric hindrance or carbocation stability).

questions.stem_md: $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2-Br}$ is classified as:
questions.solution_md: Bromine is on an sp³ carbon next to the C=C double bond: allylic — option (a). A vinylic halide (b) would have Br on the sp² carbon itself.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2CH(Cl)CH3}$ is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain has five carbons. Numbering from either end gives the locants 2 and 4, so the tie is broken alphabetically: chloro comes before methyl and gets the lower number — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these haloalkanes undergoes nucleophilic substitution most readily, other factors being equal?
questions.solution_md: The C–I bond is the longest and weakest (about 234 kJ mol⁻¹), so iodide is the best leaving group — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? 1,2-Dibromoethane is a geminal dihalide.
questions.solution_md: False. The two bromine atoms are on adjacent carbons, so it is a vicinal (vic) dihalide; a geminal dihalide has both on the same carbon, e.g. 1,1-dibromoethane.

questions.stem_md: In a C–X bond, the carbon atom carries a partial ___ charge because the halogen is more electronegative.
questions.solution_md: Carbon is δ+ (partial **positive**) and the halogen δ−.

questions.stem_md: Match each structure with its IUPAC name.
questions.solution_md: Allyl chloride is 3-chloroprop-1-ene; benzyl chloride is (chloromethyl)benzene; ethylidene chloride is 1,1-dichloroethane; tert-butyl bromide is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

questions.stem_md: Draw (or write) the structures of 1-bromo-4-chlorobut-2-ene and 1,4-dibromobenzene, and classify the C–Br bond in each.

answer.model_answer_md: 1-Bromo-4-chlorobut-2-ene is $\ce{BrCH2-CH=CH-CH2Cl}$: the C–Br carbon is sp³ and next to C=C, so it is an **allylic** halide. 1,4-Dibromobenzene has two Br on opposite carbons of a benzene ring: each C–Br is an **aryl** halide bond (sp² carbon).

questions.solution_md: Write the chain or ring, then check the hybridisation of the carbon bearing Br.

questions.stem_md: Which reagent converts ethanol into chloroethane with only gaseous by-products, so that the product is easy to purify?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C2H5OH + SOCl2 -> C2H5Cl + SO2 + HCl}$: SO₂ and HCl escape as gases — option (c). PCl₅ leaves POCl₃, PCl₃ leaves H₃PO₃, and Lucas reagent leaves water.

questions.stem_md: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: With peroxide, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch effect): Br goes to the terminal carbon — option (b). Without peroxide, 2-bromopropane (a) forms.

questions.stem_md: In the Finkelstein reaction, chloroethane is converted to iodoethane using sodium iodide in dry acetone. Why does the reaction go almost to completion?

options.text_md: Sodium chloride is insoluble in dry acetone and precipitates, removing a product.
Iodide is a weaker nucleophile than chloride.
The C–I bond is stronger than the C–Cl bond.

questions.solution_md: NaCl precipitates from acetone, so by Le Chatelier’s principle the equilibrium shifts forward — option (a). The C–I bond is in fact weaker (d).

questions.stem_md: Aniline is converted into bromobenzene by:

options.text_md: diazotisation with NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K, then warming with CuBr/HBr
treating with NaBr in dry acetone

questions.solution_md: Sandmeyer reaction: the diazonium group is replaced by Br using CuBr — option (b). Bromine water (a) gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Propene gives 2-bromopropane with HBr, but 1-bromopropane with HBr in the presence of a peroxide.

**Reason (R):** In the presence of peroxide, HBr adds by a free-radical mechanism in which the more stable secondary radical is formed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The Br· radical adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary radical, so Br ends up on C1; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each conversion with its named reaction.
questions.solution_md: CuCl on a diazonium salt: Sandmeyer; NaI/acetone: Finkelstein; AgF: Swarts; Na in dry ether: Wurtz.

questions.stem_md: Write equations, with conditions, for preparing (a) chloroethane from ethanol using thionyl chloride, (b) chlorobenzene from benzene, (c) fluoromethane from bromomethane. State one advantage of the method in (a).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{C2H5OH + SOCl2 ->[pyridine] C2H5Cl + SO2 + HCl}$; advantage: SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, so the chloroethane is obtained pure.

(b) $\ce{C6H6 + Cl2 ->[FeCl3] C6H5Cl + HCl}$ (in the dark, anhydrous catalyst).

(c) $\ce{CH3Br + AgF -> CH3F + AgBr}$ (Swarts reaction).

questions.solution_md: Thionyl chloride, Lewis-acid chlorination, Swarts exchange.

questions.stem_md: Which has the highest boiling point?

options.text_md: All three boil at the same temperature

questions.solution_md: The isomers have equal mass; the unbranched chain has the largest surface area and strongest van der Waals forces — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A few drops of a colourless haloalkane are added to water in a test tube and sink to the bottom. The haloalkane is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Bromo- and iodoalkanes are denser than water, because heavy halogen atoms add mass without much volume — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Haloalkanes are only very slightly soluble in water.

**Reason (R):** Haloalkanes are non-polar molecules.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: haloalkanes are polar. They dissolve poorly because the energy needed to break the hydrogen bonds of water is not released by forming new, weaker attractions — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bromoethane has a higher boiling point than chloroethane.

**Reason (R):** Bromine is less electronegative than chlorine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the higher boiling point is due to the greater mass and polarisability of bromine (stronger van der Waals forces), not to its lower electronegativity — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic substitution more easily than chloroethane.

**Reason (R):** The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene has partial double-bond character because of resonance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: chlorobenzene is much less reactive. R is true, and is in fact the main reason for its low reactivity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The three dichlorobenzenes have similar boiling points, but 1,4-dichlorobenzene melts at 323 K while the 1,2- and 1,3-isomers melt below 260 K. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Boiling depends mainly on attractions in the liquid, which are similar for the three isomers. Melting also depends on how well molecules pack in the crystal. The symmetrical para isomer packs closely in the solid lattice, so more energy is needed to break it and its melting point is much higher.

questions.solution_md: Symmetry and crystal packing.

marking_scheme.step: Symmetrical para isomer packs better in the crystal
More energy needed to melt; boiling unaffected by packing

questions.stem_md: A haloalkane reacts with hydroxide ions. Doubling [OH⁻] doubles the rate, and an optically active reactant gives a product of opposite configuration. The mechanism is:
questions.solution_md: Rate depends on the nucleophile (second order) and configuration is inverted: SN2 — option (d). SN1 (a) would be independent of [OH⁻] and give racemisation.

questions.stem_md: Which compound reacts fastest with aqueous NaOH by the SN2 mechanism?
questions.solution_md: SN2 needs backside attack; the least crowded carbon reacts fastest: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3° — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Arrange in increasing order of reactivity by the SN1 mechanism: (CH₃)₃CCl, CH₃Cl, (CH₃)₂CHCl, CH₃CH₂Cl.
questions.solution_md: SN1 rate follows carbocation stability, which increases with the number of alkyl groups on the positive carbon: methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary — option (a). (b) is the SN2 order.

questions.stem_md: Bromoethane is warmed with ethanolic silver cyanide. The main organic product is:
questions.solution_md: AgCN is mainly covalent, so the lone pair on nitrogen attacks: an isocyanide forms — option (c). KCN (ionic) gives the nitrile (a).

questions.stem_md: A student wants to make nitroethane from iodoethane. Which reagent should be used?
questions.solution_md: With AgNO₂ the nitrogen attacks, giving R–NO₂ (nitroalkane); KNO₂ gives the alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O (b) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An optically active sample of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane is hydrolysed in aqueous acetone by the SN1 mechanism. The product is:

options.text_md: largely racemic, because the planar carbocation is attacked from both faces
entirely the alcohol with retained configuration
optically active, because the carbocation is chiral

questions.solution_md: The carbocation intermediate is planar (sp²), so water attacks either face almost equally: mainly a racemic product — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tertiary butyl bromide reacts with aqueous NaOH faster by SN1 than by SN2.

**Reason (R):** Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by three alkyl groups, while the backside of a tertiary carbon is crowded.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; easy carbocation formation favours SN1 while steric crowding blocks SN2, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Allyl chloride is hydrolysed more readily than 1-chloropropane by the SN1 route.

**Reason (R):** The C–Cl bond in allyl chloride is part of a vinylic system with partial double-bond character.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the allyl carbocation is stabilised by resonance. R is false: the chlorine in allyl chloride is on an sp³ carbon (allylic), not vinylic; there is no partial double-bond character in its C–Cl bond — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For an SN2 reaction, rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]. By what factor does the rate change if [RX] is tripled and [Nu⁻] is doubled?
questions.solution_md: New rate $= k(3[\ce{RX}])(2[\ce{Nu-}])$, a factor of $3 \times 2 = 6$.

questions.stem_md: For an SN1 reaction, rate = k[RX]. By what factor does the rate change if [RX] is doubled and [Nu⁻] is tripled?
questions.solution_md: The nucleophile is not in the rate law, so only the doubling of RX matters: factor $2 \times 1 = 2$.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a chiral molecule? Identify the chiral compound among 2-bromobutane and 1-bromobutane, and say why.

answer.model_answer_md: In SN2, the hydroxide ion attacks the carbon from the side opposite the bromine. In a single step, the O–C bond forms as the C–Br bond breaks, through a transition state in which carbon is partly bonded to both and the three hydrogens lie in a plane. In SN1, the C–Br bond of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane first breaks slowly to give a tertiary carbocation and bromide; then water or hydroxide attacks the planar carbocation quickly. Primary halides have an unhindered carbon for backside attack and form unstable carbocations, so they react by SN2; tertiary halides are too crowded for backside attack but form stable carbocations, so they react by SN1.

answer.model_answer_md: An alcohol can be converted to a chloroalkane with HCl and anhydrous ZnCl₂, with phosphorus pentachloride (giving POCl₃ and HCl), or with thionyl chloride (giving SO₂ and HCl). Thionyl chloride is best because both by-products are gases that escape, leaving the pure product. In the Finkelstein reaction, a chloro- or bromoalkane is heated with NaI in dry acetone to give an iodoalkane; NaCl or NaBr precipitates, so the reaction goes to completion. In the Swarts reaction, a chloro- or bromoalkane is heated with AgF, Hg₂F₂ or SbF₃ to give a fluoroalkane, for example CH₃Br + AgF → CH₃F + AgBr. Boiling points rise from fluoro to iodo because molecular mass and size, and hence van der Waals forces, increase. Branching makes molecules more compact, reducing the surface area of contact and the van der Waals forces, so the boiling point falls.

answer.model_answer_md: A lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the benzene ring, so in the resonance hybrid the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character; it is shorter and stronger and is not easily broken. The carbon is sp², and the phenyl cation needed for SN1 is unstable. Conversion to phenol needs aqueous NaOH at about 623 K and 300 atm, followed by acidification. A para nitro group withdraws electron density and stabilises the negatively charged intermediate formed when the nucleophile adds, so substitution becomes much easier at lower temperatures. In electrophilic substitution, chlorine withdraws electrons by its −I effect, making the ring less reactive than benzene (deactivating), but its +R effect increases electron density at the ortho and para positions, so the electrophile enters there. Nitration gives 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene and 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, the para isomer being major.
